title: In 1995, an 84-Foot Wall of Water Hit an Oil Rig Out of Nowhere

scenes.text: In 1995, an 84 foot wall of water hit an oil rig.
New Year's Day, North Sea. A laser on an oil platform was measuring waves.
The sea was running about 39 feet. Then one wave came through at 84. Twice the size of its neighbours.
For centuries sailors described walls of water from nowhere. Scientists called it folklore.

scenes.text: This was the first rogue wave ever caught by an instrument. The myth was real.
Eighty four feet. Out of nowhere. The rig survived with minor damage.

description:
On January 1, 1995, a wave 84 feet (25.6 metres) high struck the Draupner oil platform in the North Sea.
A downward-pointing laser recorded it: the surrounding sea was running about 39 feet, so the wave was more than twice the height of its neighbours. It was the first rogue wave ever measured by an instrument, proof that the giant waves sailors had reported for centuries were real. The platform suffered only minor damage.
Would you work on an oil rig? Comment below.
first_comment: Rogue waves are now thought to sink ships every year that were once written off as lost to bad weather. What's the biggest wave you've ever seen in person?
